content: Carrying a pregnancy to term is not viable in certain situations, such as when it poses significant risks to the woman’s health or life, when the pregnancy results from rape or incest, or when the fetus is non-viable. Human rights principles emphasize the right to privacy, which requires states to respect individuals' autonomy in making decisions about their sexual and reproductive health, including the choice to have an abortion. Sexual and reproductive health (SRH) services, including abortion and post-abortion care, must be provided in a manner that fully respects the privacy and confidentiality of women, girls, and other pregnant individuals. Healthcare professionals should not be mandated to report cases of abortion, as this could violate the right to privacy. Denying therapeutic abortion or requiring third-party authorization may also infringe on this right. The right to be free from torture, cruel, inhuman, and degrading treatment includes protection against forced abortion, criminalization of abortion, denial or delay of safe abortion care, and mistreatment of women seeking SRH services. Such actions can constitute gender-based violence and, in some cases, may amount to torture. Abortion services must only be provided with the free and informed consent of the individual, and states must prevent and prosecute forced abortions, including those conducted under coercive family planning policies or in conflict settings. Women with disabilities must also be able to exercise this right without discrimination. States must provide accurate, evidence-based information on SRH, including abortion, in accessible formats and languages. Educational institutions should incorporate unbiased, scientifically accurate, and age-appropriate sexuality education into their curricula. Individuals must have access to confidential and accurate abortion information, and their choice to refuse such information must be respected. Post-abortion care is a core obligation of states under the right to SRH, regardless of the legality of abortion. Such care must be provided confidentially, without discrimination, and without the threat of criminal prosecution. Accountability mechanisms are essential to protect and fulfill SRH rights. States must establish accessible, transparent, and effective systems for individuals to challenge the denial of abortion care and to seek remedies for failures in providing quality care. These mechanisms should include regular review and reform of laws and policies to remove barriers to abortion care. An enabling environment for abortion care requires addressing stigma, ensuring respectful and compassionate care, and supporting individuals and their families. Health systems must be organized to respect individuals' autonomy and incorporate their values and preferences into care. States must also address barriers such as stigma, financial costs, lack of trained providers, and inadequate resources, which disproportionately affect vulnerable groups, including those in rural areas, adolescents, unmarried individuals, and those living with HIV. Universal health coverage (UHC) must include access to safe and effective abortion care, integrated into primary healthcare systems. States must shift the financial burden of abortion care from individuals to public funding to achieve equitable access and support UHC goals.
